To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we propose two online algorithms that learn a diverse ranking based on users' clicks and that we show that these algorithms asymptotically achieve optimal worst-case performance, even if users' preferences change.

1) we introduce a new online learning problem for learning diverse rankings; 2) we present two online algorithms that learn to rank documents based on users clicking behavior, one algorithm that minimizes abandonment and one algorithm that maximizes the probability that a user finds a relevant document in the top k ranks; and 3) we show that one of our algorithms achieves optimal worst-case behavior.

(a) online learning can produce rankings that are both accurate and diverse, (b) our algorithms can be used in a variety of settings, and (c) our algorithms achieve optimal worst-case performance in the case that user interests change.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of learning to rank diverse sets of documents.
developing algorithms for learning to rank that produce rankings that satisfy user preferences.
developing online algorithms for ranking that can learn from user behavior and that produce rankings with high diversity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our algorithms are the best algorithms for the task at hand.
the two proposed algorithms are able to learn a ranking function that is able to learn a diversity of documents based on the user's click behavior.
the algorithms we proposed are able to learn diverse rankings with minimal abandonment, and are robust against changing user preferences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown how to learn a diverse ranking function that is robust to changes in users' interests, while still maximizing the probability that the user finds a relevant document in the top k results.
we present the first learning to rank algorithms that directly optimize diversity and are robust to changes in user interests.
our proposed algorithms learn diverse ranking with multi-armed-bandits and can be applied to the real-world search engine scenario.
The main takeaway from our work is that
learning to rank Web results can be formulated as a multi-armed bandit problem.
the diversity of a ranking can be optimized directly from user behavior.
it is possible to directly learn to rank documents in a diverse manner.
